names: Ross Lake boat crossing, Lightning Creek and the abandoned Freezeout Creek trail to the north-face glacier
Provincial park approach from the north over Frosty Mountain to Crow Creek

approach_variants.name: Ross Lake boat crossing, Lightning Creek and the abandoned Freezeout Creek trail to the north-face glacier
approach_variants.notes:
This is the approach that stays inside the United States, and it is a multi-day trudge rather than a walk.

From the highway pullout above the dam a short spur trail drops to the lake shore. Cross by water taxi or by a boat you portage down that spur, and land near the head of the lake where the Lightning Creek trail begins. Follow it, then pick up the abandoned and increasingly brushy Freezeout Creek trail, whose worst navigation is the steep rock-and-alder diagonal immediately above the junction — intermittent orange flagging marks it. The cabin at about 3,600 ft is a good waypoint and an emergency shelter; tread mostly dies around 4,200 ft.

The lower corridor is national recreation area and camping there needs a park backcountry permit; the upper part is wilderness with a free self-issue permit.

From the upper basin, cross round to the north side and onto the glacier at the foot of the wall. The glacier itself is mellow and allows easy travel.
approach_variants.season: Roughly late June through September, once the approach glacier and moraine are passable
hazards: Several unmarked routes on one fourteen-hundred-foot wall; position under the summit is the only identifier
Awkward bergschrund or moat at the start of the climbing
Rockfall on the lower wall; the first pitch exists mainly to escape the fall line
Dirt and moss-filled cracks through the middle section and teetering blocks near the top
Multi-day approach with no cell coverage and an extremely slow retreat
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The north face is a wall of granite ribs, gullies and couloirs about fourteen hundred feet high, holding ice or the remnants of it, with a glacier at its foot. It carries several routes and they are not marked, so identification is by POSITION AGAINST THE SUMMIT and nothing else.

THE TEST IS SIMPLE AND IT IS THE WHOLE IDENTIFICATION: this route takes the CENTRAL BUTTRESS, and that buttress sits DIRECTLY BELOW THE SUMMIT. Stand back on the glacier, find the summit on the skyline, and drop a plumb line from it. The buttress under that line is this route. If the summit is off to one side from where you are standing, you are under a different climb.

Getting onto it is the second problem. Expect an awkward BERGSCHRUND OR MOAT where the glacier meets the rock, and start with easy fifth-class ground whose purpose is to get out of the ROCKFALL LINE rather than to climb anything — that first pitch is a position move, not a feature.

CONFIRM ON PITCH TWO, because it arrives fast and it is unmistakable: the crux comes almost immediately, mid-fifth-class face climbing hard enough that the first ascent used a short aid move to pass it. A wall this size whose hardest pitch is the second one is unusual, and it is the strongest evidence you are on line.

The middle of the route then traverses out of a dihedral on a tricky flake and takes a roof on the LEFT via cracks and stemming, over slabs that needed heavy cleaning of dirt and moss. After about five pitches the route gains the ridge proper and the rock quality improves markedly, with one short harder hand-and-fist crack. The final technical pitch picks its way around teetering blocks, and then moderate snow slopes run the last four hundred feet to the top.

NEGATIVE MARKER: if your line starts in a blocky set of face holds beside a gully or chimney at the LEFT EDGE of the buttress, you are on the neighbouring route at the buttress's left margin, and higher up it follows a distinctive yellow quartz dyke that this route does not touch.

Descent is not the climb reversed. Walk off the south side and the east ridge back toward camp.

approach_variants.name: Provincial park approach from the north over Frosty Mountain to Crow Creek
approach_variants.notes:
READ THE LEGAL POINT FIRST. This line walks in from the provincial park on the northern side and then crosses the international boundary cross-country. That is not a lawful crossing. Away from a port of entry it requires prior arrangement with the border authority, the corridor is patrolled, and casual parties cannot simply walk over. It is the first-ascent line, not a recommendation.

It starts from the lake in the provincial park, climbs up and over Frosty Mountain, descends into the next creek basin to the south, traverses to the divide, and drops into the Crow Creek drainage below the peak's north face. The first ascent camped on the only dry spot on the ridge, roughly two-thirds of the way down toward the glacier.

The wholly lawful alternatives are the boat crossing and abandoned creek trail from the east, or the crest trail from the west.
hazards: The described approach crosses the international boundary cross-country and is not a lawful crossing
Cross-country travel over a mountain and two drainage divides with one dry camp on the ridge
Awkward bergschrund or moat at the base of the wall
Rockfall on the lower face
Retreat from anywhere on this trip is measured in days
approach_variants.baseFinding:
However you reach it, the glacier at the foot of the wall is the same and the identification is the same.

Come down the ridge from camp to the glacier, which is mellow enough to walk. Then stand back far enough to see the whole face at once — this is the step the approach itself makes easy from this side, because you descend toward the wall rather than arriving under it, and a descending approach gives you the one view that settles the route.

FROM THAT VIEW, DROP A PLUMB LINE FROM THE SUMMIT. The buttress under it is this route. The face carries several other lines and none is marked; being under the summit is the identification.

Watch for an awkward BERGSCHRUND OR MOAT where the glacier meets the rock. The first pitch is easy fifth-class ground taken to escape the ROCKFALL LINE rather than for the climbing, and the crux arrives at once on pitch two — face climbing hard enough that a short aid move was used on the first ascent.

NEGATIVE MARKER: a start in blocky face holds beside a gully or chimney at the LEFT EDGE of the buttress is the neighbouring route, which follows a yellow quartz dyke higher up.

Second negative marker, and it applies from the moment you leave camp: the boundary clearing is a visible cut line on this ground and it is not a route. The summit sits about a mile south of it.

Descent is the south side and the east ridge, unroped third and fourth-class ground from the top of the technical climbing, back toward camp.

names: Ross Lake boat crossing, Lightning Creek and the abandoned Freezeout Creek trail to the north-face glacier
Provincial park approach from the north over Frosty Mountain to Crow Creek

approach_variants.name: Ross Lake boat crossing, Lightning Creek and the abandoned Freezeout Creek trail to the north-face glacier
approach_variants.notes:
The approach that stays inside the United States, and much the longer of the two.

From the highway pullout above the dam, a spur trail drops to the lake shore; cross by water taxi or by a boat portaged down it, and land near the head of the lake. Follow the Lightning Creek trail, then the abandoned and increasingly brushy Freezeout Creek trail. The steep rock-and-alder diagonal immediately above the trail junction is the hardest navigation on the whole walk; look for intermittent orange flagging. The cabin at about 3,600 ft is a waypoint and an emergency shelter, and tread mostly disappears around 4,200 ft.

Camping in the lower corridor needs a park backcountry permit; the upper part is wilderness with a free self-issue permit.

From the upper basin, work round to the north side and onto the glacier at the foot of the wall, which is mellow enough for easy travel.
approach_variants.season: Summer; the documented ascent was made in early August
hazards: At least four unmarked lines on one wall, two of them starting close together on the same buttress
Awkward bergschrund or moat at the base of the climbing
Roughly half the pitches are at the upper end of the grade, with the crux on a corner low down
Descent by the east ridge and a snow finger, not by reversing the climb
Multi-day approach and a retreat measured in days
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The face is about fourteen hundred feet of granite ribs, gullies and couloirs above a glacier and it carries several routes with nothing marked. Do not identify by name; identify by feature.

FIRST, PLACE THE CENTRAL BUTTRESS. Stand back on the glacier and find the summit, then look at the buttress directly beneath it — that is the neighbouring route, and this line is NOT on it. This route takes the LEFT MARGIN of that buttress system, so you want to be off to the left of the plumb line from the summit.

SECOND, FIND THE GULLY OR CHIMNEY AT THE BUTTRESS'S LEFT EDGE. The start is in the BLOCKY LINE OF FACE HOLDS JUST LEFT OF IT. Blocky face holds, immediately left of a gully or chimney, at the left edge of the buttress: that is the whole identification at the ground. The first pitch is long, mostly low fifth class, with a wide crack near its end.

THIRD, AND THIS IS THE CONFIRMATION HIGHER UP THAT NOTHING ELSE ON THE FACE GIVES YOU: this route follows a DISTINCTIVE YELLOW QUARTZ DYKE up the wall to avoid the dirtier rock either side of it. A yellow band running up the granite is not a subtle feature. If you never meet one, you are on a different climb.

Watch for an awkward BERGSCHRUND OR MOAT where the glacier meets the rock.

NEGATIVE MARKERS, and they matter because two of the neighbours are hard: if the summit is directly overhead from your belay and your second pitch is desperate face climbing wanting an aid move, you are on the central buttress line. And the face's original route and at least two others also exist here, so the honest rule is that anything without the yellow dyke above it is not this.

Descent is not the route reversed and not a rappel: take the east ridge from the top to an obvious col, then a snow finger back down toward the approach glacier and basin.

approach_variants.name: Provincial park approach from the north over Frosty Mountain to Crow Creek
approach_variants.notes:
READ THE LEGAL POINT FIRST. This approach walks in from the provincial park on the northern side and crosses the international boundary cross-country. That is not a lawful crossing. Away from a port of entry it needs prior arrangement with the border authority, the corridor is patrolled, and casual parties cannot simply walk over. It is recorded because it is the commonly published line and the shorter of the two, not as a recommendation.

As described, it takes the old trail along the creek to the boundary, then leaves the trail and travels cross-country south past Frosty Mountain, descending through the next creek basin and over the divide into the drainage below the peak's north face, finishing at the toe of the glacier.

The lawful alternatives are the boat crossing and abandoned creek trail from the east, or the crest trail from the west, both of which are considerably longer.
approach_variants.season: Summer, once the divide traverse is clear enough to travel
hazards: The described approach crosses the international boundary cross-country and is not a lawful crossing
Cross-country travel over a mountain and a drainage divide to reach the glacier
Awkward bergschrund or moat at the base of the wall
Several unmarked routes on one face, two of them on the same buttress
Descent by the east ridge and a snow finger rather than the way you came up
approach_variants.baseFinding:
Whichever way you arrive, the glacier is the same and so is the identification, and this side has one advantage worth using: you come DOWN toward the wall, which gives you the whole face in one view before you are under it. Take that view rather than sorting the routes out from the bergschrund.

From back on the glacier, find the summit and note the buttress directly under it — that is the neighbouring line and it is not this one. This route is on the LEFT MARGIN of the same buttress system.

The ground marker is a GULLY OR CHIMNEY at the buttress's left edge, with the route starting in the BLOCKY LINE OF FACE HOLDS JUST LEFT OF IT. The confirmation above is a YELLOW QUARTZ DYKE, which the line follows deliberately to stay on clean rock and away from the dirtier granite either side. Yellow band, left margin, blocky start beside a chimney: those three together are the route.

Expect an awkward bergschrund or moat at the transition from ice to rock.

NEGATIVE MARKERS. Directly under the summit with a very hard second pitch means the central buttress line. No yellow dyke anywhere above you means one of the other lines on this face, of which there are several and none is marked.

Second negative marker and it is not about climbing: the boundary clearing is a visible cut line across this ground. It is not a route and it is not a shortcut.

Descent is the east ridge to an obvious col and then a snow finger back to the glacier and basin.

names: Boulder Creek and the sheepherder's trail to the south basin — the non-glacier line
Boulder Pass and the Walrus Glacier — the glacier line

approach_variants.name: Boulder Creek and the sheepherder's trail to the south basin — the non-glacier line
approach_variants.notes: Start at the White River trailhead at the end of White River Road, FR 6400, at about 2,300 ft; a Northwest Forest Pass is needed. Walk the White River trail #1507 about four flat miles — one party gained all of three hundred feet in a little over an hour — to the Boulder Creek trail #1562 junction. Turn east up Boulder Creek. At about the 5,000 ft level, roughly four and a half miles up this trail, pick up an old sheepherder's trail heading west and follow it to around 5,600 to 5,700 ft. Note that published mileages on this stretch do not reconcile cleanly between sources, so navigate by elevation and by the basin rather than by a mile count. There is a faint path that contours, crosses the creek and climbs the west side of Boulder Creek, firming up into decent tread as it gains the slope. Leave the sheepherder's trail in the basin above Boulder Creek around 5,700 ft and climb open heather north-north-west to the southern ridge running off Clark's south-east peak, Point 8373. Car to summit is given as about eleven and a half miles one way with roughly 6,500 ft of gain, and essentially every party camps in the Boulder Creek basin rather than trying it in a day.
hazards: Getting cliffed out on the spur while looking for a gully that is really a ledge
Unbridged Boulder Creek crossing, cold and thigh-deep early season and sometimes braided
Losing the sheepherder's trail — it is notoriously hard to find from the White River trail
Heavy mosquitoes on the valley walk
No water above the Boulder Creek basin
approach_variants.baseFinding: EVERYTHING TURNS ON ONE FEATURE AND IT IS MISDESCRIBED BY ITS OWN NAME. Published descriptions call it the one and only easy gully breaching the ridge — the way down off the spur into Clark's south basin — and it leaves the crest at about 7,200 to 7,300 ft. The correction, from a climber who found it: it is Class 2, and it FEELS MORE LIKE A SLOPING LEDGE THAN A GULLY. Parties hunting for a defined cleft walk past it and get cliffed out. Two accounts both put it at 7,200 ft and both anchor it to the south spur of Point 8373, so the elevation is the reliable half of the identification and the word gully is the unreliable half. The positional cue that puts you in the right place to look: there is a flattish section of the spur at 7,200 ft that is reached easily on scree and grass. Stand on that flat and you can see the south slope of Clark, which looks easy — and it is. The difficulty is purely in getting DOWN to it, which is what the ledge is for. Drop a couple of hundred feet down that ledge, then contour the upper south basin on broken rock and patches of permanent snow to the final south ridge and a short Class 3 scramble to the top. A note on names before you cross-reference anything: the Walrus Glacier is shown as the Clark Glacier on maps. They are one feature with two names.

approach_variants.name: Boulder Pass and the Walrus Glacier — the glacier line
approach_variants.notes:
Approach identically to Boulder Basin: White River trail #1507 four miles to the Boulder Creek trail #1562, then up into the open basin at roughly 5,300 ft, about five to six hours and three thousand feet from the car. That basin is the camp.

From camp, climb north-east to Boulder Pass at about 6,300 to 6,330 ft. Drop down steep snow on the far side, then climb to a bench at about 6,700 ft on Clark's eastern arm.

THE BENCH IS WHERE YOU ROPE UP. Do it there, before you go anywhere, because of what comes next.
approach_variants.season: Roughly late Jun-Sep, on the earlier side while the crevasses are still bridged
hazards: Crevasses and snowbridges on the lower Walrus Glacier
Steep snow on the far side of Boulder Pass
No view of the glacier until you have committed around the eastern arm
Unbridged Boulder Creek ford lower down
The 7,200 ft south-basin gully is a landmark for a different route and will mislead you here
approach_variants.baseFinding:
YOU CANNOT SEE THE WALRUS GLACIER UNTIL YOU ARE COMMITTED TO IT. From the 6,700 ft bench you wrap around Clark's eastern arm, and only then does the glacier come into view for the first time. That is why the bench is the roping-up point rather than the glacier's edge — there is no convenient stopping place once you are round the corner.

The entry is specific and it is not the middle of the toe: go up a moderately steep chute on the LEFT, SOUTHERN margin of the glacier. Expect to step over several narrow crevasses and, in at least one recorded year, to cross a snowbridge over a large one.

Once on the gentle upper glacier the summit wedge is visible in the distance and the navigation problem is over. The finish skirts the upper south face of that wedge on a steep snowfield and ends with a short scramble onto the summit rocks — about six hours from camp.

NEGATIVE MARKER, and this one matters because it would send you to the wrong landmark entirely: the famous one-and-only-easy-gully at 7,200 ft belongs to the SOUTH BASIN route, not to this one. If you are on the Walrus you never touch it. A published page titled for the Walrus Glacier in fact describes the south-basin line in its turn-by-turn, so read carefully which route a description is actually walking.

names: White River, St Elmo Pass and Curtis Ridge

approach_variants.name: Mowich Lake and Spray Park
approach_variants.notes:
From Mowich Lake, follow the trail roughly 3 miles to Spray Park, then climb the lower slopes of Ptarmigan Ridge. The ridge narrows above Observation Rock; continue along it until you find bivouac sites. High camp is normally somewhere between about 9,500 and 10,300 ft, at the point where Ptarmigan Ridge runs into the main cone below the Liberty Cap icefall. Higher camps are worth the extra carry because they let you look at the bergschrund and pick a line the evening before.

This is the shorter of the two approaches, and it is the one most parties would choose if the road cooperated. The Mowich Lake road is unpaved, seasonal and typically opens later than the White River road — mid-summer rather than late spring in a normal snow year. Since the route is best when there is still winter snow on it, the road schedule is a structural problem with this variant rather than an occasional inconvenience. Check the road's status before planning around it.

The approach to high camp is normally split over two days.
approach_variants.season: May-Jul; the road to Mowich Lake is closed indefinitely, so this start cannot currently be reached by car
hazards: Bergschrund crossing off the Mowich Glacier, conditions-dependent
Loose rock descending from high camp onto the glacier
Icefall exposure below the Liberty Cap icefall near high camp
Verglassed rock and water ice on the upper mixed ground
Committing position with a descent by a different route — plan the carry-over
approach_variants.baseFinding:
High camp is not the start of the climbing — and the mistake this route invites is treating the ridge you camped on as the ridge you climb.

From camp at around 10,000–10,300 ft you DESCEND, on loose rock or steep snow, onto the Mowich Glacier. If you are gaining height straight out of the tents along a rocky crest, you are still on the approach ridge.

The first real feature is the bergschrund, usually crossed by a bridge just left of a rock outcropping near the centre. Above it the climbing is 40–45 degree snow for about 1,000 ft, and it ends in an obvious way: you run up under large rock cliffs. That is the signal to traverse left into an hourglass-shaped snow face rather than to keep going up.

The next decision point is a rock buttress at about 11,500 ft, where the route splits — left and around toward Liberty Cap between the buttress and the icefall, or right through mixed ground, a minor rock rib and the left margin of the Mowich Face to a second rock gully. Either way there is a short section of real rock or mixed climbing above 12,000 ft; if you have got that high on pure snow, you have probably drifted onto the Liberty Cap glacier ground.

Descent is normally the Emmons, not this route.

approach_variants.name: White River, St Elmo Pass and Curtis Ridge
approach_variants.notes:
Follow the Glacier Basin trail from White River Campground and leave it for St Elmo Pass (7,400 ft), about 4 miles in. Descend onto the Winthrop Glacier and traverse west toward Curtis Ridge, holding elevation. Cross Curtis Ridge, cross the Carbon Glacier, then climb moderate snow slopes onto Ptarmigan Ridge below its 10,200 ft high point, where there are good bivouac sites.

This is the long way around the north side of the mountain and it shares its first half with the Liberty Ridge approach. It usually implies a car shuttle or, more often, a carry-over with descent by the Emmons–Winthrop back to White River — which conveniently is also the standard descent from the route itself.
approach_variants.season: Available earlier in the season than the Mowich Lake road, at the cost of a much longer approach
hazards: Serac discharge from Willis Wall on the traverse between Curtis Ridge and the Carbon
Crevasse fields on the Winthrop and Carbon glaciers
Long committing traverse with no quick exit
Same bergschrund and upper mixed-ground hazards as the Mowich approach
approach_variants.baseFinding:
Up to the Carbon Glacier this is the Liberty Ridge approach, and the same negative markers apply: leave the Glacier Basin trail rather than walking into Glacier Basin, lose height off St Elmo Pass rather than gaining it, and treat the ground under Willis Wall as a crossing rather than a place to stand.

Where it diverges: instead of turning up the Carbon toward the toe of Liberty Ridge, you continue west across the Carbon and climb snow onto Ptarmigan Ridge below its 10,200 ft high point. If you find yourself gaining a defined rib immediately above the Carbon with Willis Wall right behind you, you have stopped at Liberty Ridge — Ptarmigan is further round to the west.

Once camped on Ptarmigan Ridge the start of the climbing is the same as from the Mowich side: down off the ridge onto the Mowich Glacier, then the bergschrund, then 40–45 degree snow to the base of the rock cliffs.

wa_mount_rainier_ptarmigan_ridge.approach: The road to Mowich Lake is closed indefinitely: the Fairfax Bridge on SR 165 was permanently closed in April 2025, and there is no public access to Mowich Lake even on foot, so the White River side is the only start a car can currently reach. Historically approached either from the west via Mowich Lake (shorter) or from the east via White River Campground (longer, typically requiring a car shuttle or carryover with descent via the Emmons Glacier). Which of the two is actually available is a seasonal question rather than a fixed one: the Mowich Lake road is summer-only and in a normal year opens well after this route comes into condition, so the shorter approach and the season rarely line up. The White River side is reachable earlier, at the cost of a much longer walk. Check the road status before planning around Mowich Lake.

names: Up the valley from the landing, then off-trail into the lake basin
Over the pass at the head of the river road and down to the lake from the west

approach_variants.name: Up the valley from the landing, then off-trail into the lake basin
approach_variants.notes:
There is no road to this side of the peak. Reach the valley by ferry or floatplane, then take the valley road or the park shuttle to a campground and pick up the valley trail from there. The lake below the peak is reached by leaving that trail and pushing off-trail and unmarked into the basin - a steep, poorly marked fisherman's path at best, and map-and-compass travel above it. Figure a full day of travel each way and plan on two or three days with a camp at or below the lake.

One caution about the paperwork rather than the ground: the written descriptions of this approach and the recorded waypoints for it name different drainages for that off-trail section, and the recorded distances do not match the recorded positions. Plan the departure point from current maps and imagery rather than from any single written description.
approach_variants.season: Midsummer through early autumn, once the basin is walkable and the valley road and trail are open
hazards: reaching the valley at all depends on a ferry or floatplane and a shuttle
an unmarked off-trail push into the basin with no reliable path
loose unconsolidated talus and steep heather benches with unstable footing
no tread to follow on the descent, on ground where every slope looks the same
an exposed class 3 finish off the ridge
conflicting records of the approach drainage, so the departure point must be planned from maps
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE LAKE IS THE ANCHOR AND THE ROUTE IS READ FROM IT. The lake sits immediately NORTH-EAST of the summit, so from the water the peak is to the south-west.

LEAVE THE LAKE BASIN AND GAIN THE BROAD BASIN AND SLOPES DIRECTLY ABOVE IT ON THE SOUTH SIDE, aiming for the LOW POINT ON THE SUMMIT RIDGE rather than for the summit itself. There are no cairns and no path here; the terrain is the navigation.

THE GROUND CONFIRMS ITSELF AS YOU GAIN HEIGHT: loose unconsolidated talus interspersed with heather benches on a steep grade, with unstable footing and no established tread. NOTE YOUR ASCENT LINE, because on the descent one talus-and-heather slope looks exactly like the next and there is nothing to follow.

THE FINISH IS THE TEST THAT YOU CHOSE THE RIGHT SIDE. From the ridge the last stretch to the top is a short EXPOSED CLASS 3 SCRAMBLE. IF THE GROUND ABOVE YOU IS A STEEP CONTINUOUS SNOW LINE SPLITTING THE SUMMIT BLOCK, YOU HAVE COME ROUND ONTO THE NORTH SIDE AND ARE UNDER THE COULOIR ROUTE, which is a different proposition entirely and wants an axe, crampons and a season this route does not.

Also confirm the peak: a similarly named summit elsewhere in the range is approached from a completely different valley. The lake immediately north-east of your summit is what identifies this one.

approach_variants.name: Over the pass at the head of the river road and down to the lake from the west
approach_variants.notes:
The lake can also be reached from the other side of the range, by climbing to the pass at about 5,392 ft at the head of the river road - or the nearby col used when the pass is corniced - and then travelling east, descending and traversing through the basin beyond to the lake at about 4,170 ft.

This avoids the ferry and the unmarked valley push entirely, at the cost of a pass crossing in each direction and a descent that has to be re-climbed at the end of the trip.
approach_variants.season: Late spring into summer, while the pass is straightforward and the basin beyond is still simple travel
hazards: a corniced pass in early season
a descent from the pass that must be re-climbed on the way out
loose talus and heather with unstable footing and no tread
an exposed class 3 finish
a basin with no path and no obvious exit seen from above
approach_variants.baseFinding:
FROM THE PASS THE TRAVEL IS EAST AND DOWNHILL TO THE LAKE, so the arrival marker is water at about 4,170 ft with the peak standing to the SOUTH-WEST of it.

FROM THE LAKE, THE SOUTH SLOPES ARE GAINED BY GOING ROUND THE PEAK, NOT UP THE SIDE FACING YOU. The face you can see from the lake is the northern one. THE ROUTE IS ON THE OPPOSITE FLANK - the broad basin and slopes above the lake basin on the south side, taken toward the low point on the summit ridge.

THE NEGATIVE MARKER IS THE SNOW LINE. IF YOU ARE LOOKING UP AT A CONTINUOUS COULOIR SPLITTING THE SUMMIT BLOCK AND ARE TEMPTED BY IT, THAT IS THE NORTH COULOIR ROUTE AND NOT THIS ONE. It is a snow climb with a different season and different equipment.

THE POSITIVE MARKERS ON THE ROUTE ARE UNDERFOOT: loose talus and heather benches on a steep grade, with no cairns, followed by an exposed class 3 scramble off the ridge to the top. Note your ascent line for the descent, because nothing here is marked.

names: Mill Creek and the Azurite Pass side
South Fork Slate Creek and the east ridge

approach_variants.name: Mill Creek and the Azurite Pass side
approach_variants.notes: This is the approach the peak is normally catalogued under and the one that pairs naturally with Azurite. It runs from Highway 20 up Canyon Creek and then Mill Creek on tread that has seen little maintenance since the mine closed, where slide alder and downed timber are the recurring complaint and parties routinely lose the path entirely for stretches. A longer alternative from the West Fork Methow trailhead reaches the same country by way of the Pacific Crest Trail and Horse Heaven Camp and is often preferred for combined trips despite the extra mileage. Camp is usually made near the old mine or in the basin above it. Note that the point long marked on maps as Mount Ballard is a lower north sub-summit; the true high point lies about 1,100 ft further south and is slightly higher.
hazards: Slide alder and downed timber on an unmaintained approach trail
Route-finding through brush pockets and broken gullies on the flank
Loose, rotten rock and exposure near the summit ridge
Snowfields into July that can require an ice axe
Open upper mountain with full lightning exposure
Very remote, with a long and difficult evacuation if injured
approach_variants.baseFinding: On this side the walking ends at the old Azurite Mine site around 5,900 ft and the brush begins immediately. The base of the climb is the open basin at roughly 6,600 ft above and east of the mine, sitting between Ballard and the ridge running out toward Azurite. You know you are in it when the timber gives out and you can see the peak's flank in one piece above you rather than through trees. That flank is the difficulty: it is not a single clean face but a patchwork of brush pockets, rock ribs and short gullies, and parties consistently find that the hard part of the day is not the scrambling but picking which gully continues, a decision that comes to a head around 7,400 ft. Read the ground rather than committing early, because a gully that closes out costs a long reversal. The obvious-looking answer is a trap: the south ridge presents as a clean continuous line from below and is blocked higher by a notch with a gendarme in it, so a party that racks up the ridge crest on sight will be turned around. The other check is on which summit you are heading for. There are two high points on this mountain, and the northern one, the one carrying the old survey mark, is the lower; keep working south along the crest until the ground stops rising. If you find yourself on the connecting ridge with Azurite you have gone north and are on the wrong end of the massif.

approach_variants.name: South Fork Slate Creek and the east ridge
approach_variants.notes: The other side of the mountain, approached from the Slate Creek road system rather than from Mill Creek, and the line most parties who climb this peak actually use. It is shorter, the forest below camp is comparatively brush-free, and the route-finding above camp is far more legible than on the Mill Creek side, at the cost of one genuinely steep step low down and some exposed ledge work near the top. Snow conditions change this route's character completely: a filled-in slot low down and firm snow in the upper cirque make for fast travel, while dry late-season conditions leave loose rock and slippery vegetation. Camp is normally made in a scree basin below the east ridge.
hazards: A steep vegetated step through the lowest cliff band, the hardest ground on the route
Exposed ledge traverse above the high saddle
Loose rock in the summit gully with a party stacked below
Steep snow in the east cirque into midsummer
Full lightning exposure on the open upper mountain
Very remote, with a long and difficult evacuation if injured
approach_variants.baseFinding: The approach has one unmistakable marker and the climb has another. Start at the locked gate on the Slate Creek road at about 3,800 ft and walk the South Fork road for roughly a mile and a half to an old vehicle bridge at about 4,000 ft; that bridge is the single positive check on the whole road walk, and if you have not crossed it you are still on the main branch. From the bridge, head south through open, brush-free forest for another mile and a half or so to a scree basin around 4,800 ft, the usual camp. From camp the route climbs through tight forest and then open scree to a shoulder on the east ridge at roughly 6,200 ft. The base of the real climbing is right there and it is easy to identify because it is the wrong colour: a steep slot of heather and grass cutting through the lowest cliff band, green vegetation in an otherwise rocky wall, and the only weakness in that band. It is the steepest ground on the route and it is the crux. Bare rock gullies to either side look more like a climb and are harder and looser, so the vegetated slot is the line. Above it stay on the rib and follow the ridge crest, then the scree slope and east cirque, to a high saddle north of the summit. From that saddle do not go straight up; traverse ledges, some of them exposed, to a narrow gully that gains the summit block.

names: Cathedral Pass and Peggy's Pond, then the east ridge and Lynch draw
Deception Pass, Marmot and Jade Lakes, and Dip Top Gap from the east

approach_variants.name: Cathedral Pass and Peggy's Pond, then the east ridge and Lynch draw
approach_variants.notes:
Hike the Cathedral Rock Trail to Nosh Nosh Wahtum (formerly Squaw Lake) at 2.5 miles, continue to Cathedral Pass at 5,550 ft, then turn left (west) onto the PCT. In less than half a mile turn right (northwest) onto Trail #1375 — do NOT follow the PCT down toward Deep Lake. Follow #1375 past Cathedral Rock to Peggy's Pond at about 5,560 ft and camp there. This is the shorter approach with the longer summit day, and it avoids the brush of the alternative.

From camp, climb to about 6,300 ft on the east ridge, then traverse BELOW the Daniel Glacier at 6,100 to 6,300 ft toward Lynch draw.

Trailhead to camp is about 2.5 to 4 hours; camp to summit 5 to 7 hours.
approach_variants.season: Jun-mid Jul, while Pea Soup Lake is frozen and the moat closed; the lake crossing gets hard once it melts
hazards: Full-width crevasses opening late in the season across the Lynch Glacier
Loose, rotten rock on the ground used to gain and leave the ice — reported as the worst hazard on the route
A moat at the rock-to-ice transition that widens through the summer
Pea Soup Lake melting out and Lynch draw flooding from mid-July
Significant glacier recession, so old descriptions understate the rock and moat work
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE ARRIVAL TEST IS A LAKE YOU WALK ACROSS. Traversing below the Daniel Glacier you come to Lynch draw and, in season, to FROZEN PEA SOUP LAKE. Walk straight across it and get onto the ice ABOVE THE LOW ROCKS on its far side. That is the base of the Lynch Glacier, and standing on the lake surface is an unambiguous confirmation you are in the right basin.

WHAT TO DO WHEN THE LAKE HAS MELTED OUT, WHICH IS THE COMMON CASE FROM MID-JULY: do not try to force the draw, which can be flooded. Instead climb the ridge SEPARATING the Daniel and Lynch glaciers for a couple of hundred yards to the FIRST MINOR NOTCH at about 6,600 ft. Drop roughly 100 ft off it to a snowfield hugging the ridge, then work climbers' LEFT via a second snowfield and rock benches onto the Lynch Glacier. First minor notch at 6,600 ft, then down 100 ft and left: that is a counted sequence rather than a described one, which is what you want in cloud.

GETTING ONTO THE ICE, IN EITHER SEASON: early, take the snow finger on climbers' RIGHT. Late, bypass on climbers' LEFT by class 3 scrambling, and expect a moat at the transition. The loose rotten rock used to reach the ice is repeatedly reported as more dangerous than the glacier itself.

AND THE TOP TELLS YOU WHICH SUMMIT IS WHICH: the glacier leads to the GAP BETWEEN THE TWO HIGHEST SUMMITS. From the notch, the WEST summit — on your RIGHT — is the true high point. Late in the season expect a detour around crevasses about two thirds of the way up.

A SCOPE NOTE THAT MATTERS TO PEAK-LIST PARTIES: reaching the upper Daniel Glacier from Peggy's Pond by the Southeast Ridge or the Hyas Creek Glacier is a scramble and is not this route.

approach_variants.name: Deception Pass, Marmot and Jade Lakes, and Dip Top Gap from the east
approach_variants.notes:
From the Deception Pass trailhead, hike to Marmot and Jade Lakes and continue to Dip Top Gap. From the gap, traverse WEST to the shoulder overlooking the Foss River drainage, then descend to the outlet of Pea Soup Lake.

This is the longer, eastern line into the same basin. It reaches the Lynch Glacier at the same point the Peggy's Pond approach does, and everything about identifying the ice is identical from the lake outlet onward.
approach_variants.season: Early season, roughly June into July, before the moat opens
hazards: Crevasses across the full width of the glacier late in the season
The moat at the rock-to-ice transition
Loose rotten rock on the class 3 bypass
A long approach over Dip Top Gap with a descent to the lake that must be reversed on the way out
approach_variants.baseFinding:
YOU ARE AIMING FOR THE OUTLET OF PEA SOUP LAKE, AND THE SHOULDER ABOVE THE FOSS RIVER IS THE WAYPOINT THAT GETS YOU THERE. From Dip Top Gap the traverse is WEST until you are on the shoulder looking down into the Foss River drainage; the descent from that shoulder lands at the lake outlet. If you are looking down into a drainage that is not the Foss, you have not traversed far enough west.

FROM THE OUTLET THE FINDING IS THE SAME AS FROM PEGGY'S POND: get onto the ice ABOVE THE LOW ROCKS at the head of the lake. Early season, take the snow finger on climbers' RIGHT; late season, bypass by class 3 on climbers' LEFT and cross the moat. Then ascend the upper glacier toward the West Pyramid and the col between the Middle and True summits.

THE NEGATIVE TEST: this route is graded third class with only minor snow and ice difficulty. If you are on steep ice, you are not on the Lynch Glacier standard line.

wa_mount_shuksan_white_salmon_glacier.approach: From the small pull-off at the old White Salmon Lodge on the Mount Baker Highway, walk around the gate and follow the old road past the lodge site for about a mile to where it ends at an old clearcut. With good snow cover, descend northeast to White Salmon Creek and follow the valley up to the toe of the White Salmon Glacier. Without it, hold your height through the clearcut and contour, losing elevation only to get around rock bands and stream crossings, to stay out of the slide alder in the valley bottom. Bivy sites sit among the rock outcrops along the eastern edge of the glacier.

approach_logistics.trailhead: White Salmon Lodge road gate (Mount Baker Highway hairpin)
approach_logistics.trailheadDirection: At the hairpin on the Mount Baker Highway near mile 52, below the ski area, park in the small pull-off at the gated road to White Salmon Lodge. Don't block the gate.
